object_types.name: Vendor
object_types.definition: A supplier from which the business procures goods or services. Identified by a unique vendor number assigned at creation.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.
Every vendor has exactly one, and no two vendors share one? ... Yes. That one I'm sure about. It's the thing we quote in every conversation with AP.

object_types.name: VendorNumber
object_types.definition: The unique system identifier assigned to a vendor upon record creation.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a vendor number, it's generated when the record is created.

object_types.name: VendorStatus
object_types.definition: The operational state of a vendor record. Every vendor is in exactly one status at any time.

source_references.excerpt: Draft, active, suspended.
Draft, active, suspended. That's what the field allows now. Every vendor is in exactly one of them.
It defaults to draft the moment the record is created.

object_types.name: LegalName
object_types.definition: The official legal name of the vendor.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address...

object_types.name: TaxId
object_types.definition: The tax identification number of the vendor. Not a unique identifier due to multi-entity filings and duplicate onboarding.

source_references.excerpt: Legal name. Tax ID. Address...
We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

object_types.name: VendorAddress
object_types.definition: A physical address associated with a vendor. A vendor may have multiple address types.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

object_types.name: SpendTier
object_types.definition: The procurement classification of a vendor based on total spending. Bronze, silver, or gold. Every vendor has a spend tier, defaulting to bronze.

source_references.excerpt: Every vendor has a tier. Bronze, silver, gold.
I'm talking about spend. Gold vendors are the ones we spend real money with, they get quarterly business reviews, better payment terms, a named relationship manager.
Every vendor gets a spend tier. Bronze by default if nobody's assessed them.

object_types.name: RiskTier
object_types.definition: The risk classification of a vendor based on a completed review. Low, medium, or high. Only vendors with a completed review have a risk tier.

source_references.excerpt: I use low, medium, high.
I'm talking about risk. Low, medium, high, based on the review -- what data they touch, what geography they operate in, whether they're a sole source.
Risk tier comes from the review, so a vendor without a review has no risk tier. Draft vendors don't have one.

object_types.name: RiskReview
object_types.definition: A compliance assessment of a vendor's risk profile. Each review has its own record with an ID, reviewer sign-off, and timestamp. A vendor accumulates multiple reviews over time; at most one is current and signed-off.

source_references.excerpt: The review is its own record. It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.
Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review.
A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one.

object_types.name: ReviewId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a risk review record.

source_references.excerpt: It has a review ID, because we need to know who signed it and when, and auditors ask.

ambiguities.description: Contact identification unclear: The fact that contacts are assigned per vendor-region combination suggests that ContactId might be composite (vendor + region + person identifier) rather than a simple auto-generated identifier. The transcript does not clarify whether each contact record has its own unique ID or whether the contact is identified by the (Vendor, Region, Person) tuple. This matters for whether Contact should have a simple reference_mode or be modeled differently.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number... A given vendor in a given region has exactly one primary contact.

ambiguities.description: Vendor-Region-Contact participation: The model captures that a vendor operating in a region has exactly one primary contact. However, it is unclear whether the Contact is a separate entity type or could be treated as an embedded value. The transcript also does not specify whether every vendor-region combination must have a contact, or only those regions in which the vendor actually operates. Current model assumes contact is optional per region (a vendor only has contacts for regions in which it operates).

source_references.excerpt: And can a vendor have no contact in a region? ... If they don't operate in that region, there's nothing there at all.

ambiguities.description: Risk review accumulation and 'current' state: The transcript distinguishes between 'exactly one completed review' (line 101) and 'several reviews of which one is current' (line 109). The model captures that at most one review is current and active vendors require a current signed-off review, but the system-level mechanics of how 'current' is marked are not specified (e.g., is there an explicit flag, or is it the most recent one?). Additionally, the transcript does not clarify whether a review must be explicitly completed and signed-off to count, or if there are intermediate states.

source_references.excerpt: Every active vendor has exactly one completed risk review... A vendor accumulates review records over time. At most one is the current one.

ambiguities.description: Spend tier vs. risk tier independence not fully formalized: While the transcript confirms that spend tier (bronze/silver/gold) and risk tier (low/medium/high) are independent fields set by different owners (lines 143-147), the model does not explicitly capture that they can coexist in any combination. The constraint is implicit (they are two separate roles on the same vendor entity), but no exclusion or dependency rules are stated.

source_references.excerpt: Two separate fields, different values, different owners... Most of our cloud providers are exactly that. Big spend, high risk.

ambiguities.description: Vendor status 'active' requires risk review, but is this a hard constraint in the system or a procedural requirement? The transcript indicates that the system blocks the transition to active without a completed review (line 91), but does not specify whether an active vendor could later lose its review status (e.g., if a review expires). The current model assumes risk tier is optional for draft vendors but mandatory for active vendors, but temporal expiry or lifecycle rules are not detailed.

source_references.excerpt: the system does enforce it -- you cannot move a vendor to active without a completed review, the transition is blocked.
If we suspend a vendor -- their review lapses, or there's a breach, or they turn up on a sanctions list...

ambiguities.description: Multiple vendor addresses not formally modeled: The transcript mentions that vendors have three address types (legal, remit-to, ship-from) and that these are frequently different and wrong (line 23). The current model represents 'VendorAddress' as a single value type that vendors can have multiple of, but does not capture address type (legal, remit-to, ship-from) as a categorization. It is unclear whether each address should be typed, whether each vendor must have all three, or whether some are mandatory and others optional.

source_references.excerpt: Address, though we have three addresses really -- remit-to, ship-from, and the legal one, which are frequently different and frequently wrong.

ambiguities.description: Purchase order creation constraint not captured: The transcript states that you cannot create a PO without picking a vendor (line 231), but does not clarify whether there is an additional constraint that the vendor must be active at creation time. The model captures that POs can only be raised against active vendors (line 243), but it is ambiguous whether this is enforced at creation or is a later check that fails at submission.

source_references.excerpt: You can't create one without picking a vendor... and you can't raise one against a vendor who isn't active.

ambiguities.description: Suspension and in-flight purchase orders remain unresolved: The transcript explicitly documents a policy conflict and parks a decision about what happens to POs when a vendor is suspended (lines 251-279). The current model does not capture any constraint or rule for this scenario because no agreed rule exists yet. If and when a decision is made (e.g., 'run-off' status allowing existing POs to complete), the model will need to be updated.

source_references.excerpt: If we suspend a vendor... what happens to the purchase orders already in flight?... Parking it explicitly: what happens to in-flight purchase orders when a vendor is suspended is undecided.

ambiguities.description: Vendor legal name uniqueness not specified: The transcript mentions that vendors are identified by vendor number, not by name (line 27), and that TaxId is not unique (line 45). However, it does not explicitly state whether legal name is unique or whether duplicate vendor names are allowed. This matters if the system should enforce name uniqueness at a semantic level.

source_references.excerpt: How do you tell one vendor from another? ... By name, usually. ... In the system, I mean.
We have vendors with the same tax ID -- different legal entities under one parent that file together, or we've onboarded the same company twice by accident and nobody's merged them.

ambiguities.description: Contact as entity type vs. value type: The model treats Contact as an entity type with its own ID and attributes (name, email, phone). However, the transcript could also support Contact as a value type or an embedded object within the Vendor-Region relationship. The decision to make Contact an entity type with ContactId is based on the Meridian incident (line 179) which shows that contacts are tracked individually and can change over time, but this is not fully explicit in how the system models them.

source_references.excerpt: Each vendor has one primary contact. Name, email, phone number... the fix was that contact stopped being a vendor-level thing and became a vendor-and-region thing.

ambiguities.description: Region set is not fixed: While the transcript lists four current regions (EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM) and the value_constraint on RegionCode restricts to these four, line 187 mentions that there is talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened yet. This suggests the region set may not be immutable and future splits or merges are possible. The model treats the four regions as a fixed value set, which may need revision if regions can be added or removed dynamically.

source_references.excerpt: Region code. EMEA, APAC, NA, LATAM. ... There's been talk of splitting EMEA but it hasn't happened.

ambiguities.description: PurchaseOrder attributes incomplete: The transcript provides only PO number, amount, and raised date as captured attributes (line 237). However, lines 235 mention that POs have many other attributes including line items, delivery dates, cost centre, and approvals. The model captures only the minimal set stated in line 237, but it is possible that for a complete picture of supplier transactions, additional attributes or related entities may be needed in the future. This is noted as acceptable scope-limiting but represents a known gap.

source_references.excerpt: There's a lot -- line items, delivery dates, cost centre, approvals... I'll take vendor, number, amount, date and we can extend later.
